Solution

Words: 257
2 OurBigBook.com
Any nonzero vector in F23​ extends to a basis. Sending one such basis to another gives an element of the general linear group, so its group action on the seven nonzero vectors is a transitive group action. Counting successive independent columns gives
∣G∣=(8−1)(8−2)(8−4)=168.
(1)
By the orbit-stabilizer theorem, the stabilizer H of a chosen nonzero vector v has order 168/7=24.
There are three two-dimensional linear subspaces containing v, corresponding to the three one-dimensional linear subspaces of F23​/⟨v⟩. The stabilizer H acts transitively on them: extend a basis of either plane beginning with v to a basis of the whole vector space. Thus the stabilizer of a flag ⟨v⟩<P has order 24/3=8.
If Q≤G has order eight, each orbit of a group action of Q on the seven nonzero vectors has size a power of two. Since seven is odd, at least one orbit of a group action has size one. Thus Q fixes a nonzero vector v. Its group action on the three planes containing v likewise has a fixed plane P. Therefore Q is contained in, and by order equals, the stabilizer of that flag. The group action of G is transitive on these flags, so all such subgroups are conjugate subgroups.
Distinct flags give distinct stabilizers. In a basis adapted to a flag, its order-eight stabilizer consists of
​100​a10​bc1​​,a,b,c∈F2​.
(2)
Its only common fixed nonzero vector is e1​. Its only invariant plane is ⟨e1​,e2​⟩: an invariant plane is the kernel of a linear map of a nonzero linear functional, and over F2​ that linear functional must be fixed; the displayed matrices have only the fixed nonzero linear functional e3∗​. Hence each subgroup specifies its flag uniquely. There are seven choices of v and three choices of P, giving
21 subgroups of order 8.​
(3)

2 OurBigBook.com
An element α is an algebraic element over F if some nonzero polynomial in F[X] vanishes at α. A field extension is an algebraic extension if each of its elements is an algebraic element over F. If [K:F]=d<∞, the d+1 vectors 1,α,…,αd are linearly dependent, producing such a polynomial. Thus every finite field extension is an algebraic extension.
The converse fails for the field of algebraic numbers Q​. It is an algebraic extension of Q by definition, but it contains primitive pth roots of unity of degree p−1 for arbitrarily large primes p, by the permitted irreducibility of the cyclotomic polynomial. The tower law would make every such degree at most [Q​:Q] if the latter were finite, a contradiction.

The polynomial X3+X+1 has no root in F2​, so it is an irreducible polynomial. The quotient ring of F2​[X] by the ideal it generates is therefore a field with eight elements. The seven nonzero elements form a group of order seven, so each satisfies x7=1 by Lagrange's theorem. Thus this field splits X7−1. A root different from one has order seven; it cannot lie in F2​ and generates this degree-three field extension, since three is prime and the tower law applies. Therefore
[K:F2​]=3.​
(7)

Solution

Words: 238
2 OurBigBook.com
Wilson's theorem states that an integer n>1 is prime if and only if (n−1)!≡−1(modn). For a prime p, every nonzero residue has a multiplicative inverse. Pair each residue with its inverse; the only self-inverse ones satisfy (a−1)(a+1)=0 in Fp​ and hence are 1,−1 (the same residue when p=2). The resulting product is −1. Conversely, if (n−1)!≡−1(modn), no divisor d of n can satisfy 1<d<n: it would divide both (n−1)! and n, so could not divide (n−1)!+1. Hence n is prime.
For a composite n≥6 which is not the square of a prime, choose a proper factorization n=ab with 1<a<b<n if possible. Both factors occur in (n−1)!, proving divisibility by n. If the initially chosen factors coincide but their common value is composite, choose a different proper divisor to obtain unequal factors; equivalently, the only composite integer all of whose proper nontrivial divisors coincide is a prime square. For n=p2≥9, the distinct factors p and 2p lie below p2 and their product is divisible by p2. Thus (n−1)!≡0(modn) for every composite n≥6.
For a prime n, write (n−1)!=kn−1. Then sin2((n−1)!π/n)=sin2(π/n), so the summand is one. For a composite n≥6 it is zero. The only remaining composite index is four, whose summand equals sin2(3π/2)/sin2(π/4)=2. Therefore the sum is the prime-counting function plus two whenever x≥4; subtraction of two gives the claimed exact formula.

A coordinate transformation is a continuously differentiable bijection from the open set U onto an open subset T(U)⊂R2, with continuously differentiable inverse. Equivalently, it is a C1 diffeomorphism; its Jacobian determinant never vanishes. The inverse function theorem supplies the local inverse, while global injectivity is an additional requirement.

The dominated convergence theorem states: if measurable fn​ converge almost everywhere to f and ∣fn​∣≤g almost everywhere for an integrable g≥0, then f is integrable and ∫fn​→∫f. In fact ∫∣fn​−f∣→0.
To derive it from the monotone convergence theorem, first prove Fatou's lemma. For nonnegative measurable hn​, the functions kN​=infn≥N​hn​ increase to liminfhn​ and satisfy ∫kN​≤infn≥N​∫hn​. Monotone convergence yields ∫liminfhn​≤liminf∫hn​.
Now ∣f∣≤g almost everywhere, so f is integrable. Apply Fatou's lemma to the nonnegative functions 2g−∣fn​−f∣, which converge almost everywhere to 2g:
2∫g≤2∫g−limsupn​∫∣fn​−f∣.
(11)
Hence ∫∣fn​−f∣→0, and ∣∫fn​−∫f∣≤∫∣fn​−f∣ proves the assertion. Common exceptional null sets may be removed at the beginning since the sequence is countable.

A topological space is compact if every open cover has a finite subcover. It is connected if it cannot be written as the union of two disjoint nonempty open subsets. It is Hausdorff if every two distinct points have disjoint open neighborhoods. These definitions apply to the space itself and, with the subspace topology, to its subsets.

a

Words: 36 Articles: 1
3 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 36
a OurBigBook.com
True. If open sets cover Y, their inverse images under the continuous surjection f cover X. Compactness of X gives a finite subcover; surjectivity then makes the corresponding finite family cover Y. This proves the compactness of a continuous image of a compact space.

b

Words: 37 Articles: 1
3 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 37
b OurBigBook.com
True. A separation of Y into two disjoint nonempty open subsets would pull back under the continuous surjection f to a separation of X. The inverse images are nonempty by surjectivity, contradicting connectedness of X. Thus a continuous image of a connected space is connected.

c

Words: 32 Articles: 1
3 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 32
c OurBigBook.com
True. The Hausdorff assumption makes {y} closed in Y. Its inverse image under the continuous map f is closed in the compact space X, and a closed subset of a compact space is compact. This is the compactness of the fiber with its subspace topology.

d

Words: 35
d OurBigBook.com
False. Take X=[0,1], Y=S1 and the surjection f(t)=e2πit. The interval is compact and connected, and the circle is Hausdorff. But f−1(1)={0,1} is a disconnected two-point subspace. Thus a continuous surjection need not have connected fibers.

e

Words: 58 Articles: 1
3 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 58
e OurBigBook.com
False. Let X be a two-point set with the indiscrete topology, let Y be a one-point space, and let f be the unique map. The space X is finite and hence compact; its only nonempty open subset is all of X, so it is connected. It is not Hausdorff, whereas Y is Hausdorff and f is a continuous surjection.

4 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 117
a OurBigBook.com
For the canonical surjection p:X→X/∼, define a subset W of X/∼ to be open exactly when p−1(W) is open in X. This is the quotient topology. The empty set and the whole quotient have open inverse images. Moreover inverse images commute with arbitrary unions and finite intersections, so the corresponding axioms of a topology follow directly from those on X.
The map p need not be an open map. For example, on X=R identify every point of [0,1] to one point and leave all other classes singletons. The set U=(−1/2,1/2) is open, but
p−1(p(U))=(−1/2,1]
(14)
is not open. The definition of the quotient topology therefore shows that p(U) is not open. The obstruction is that saturating an open set by equivalence classes need not preserve openness.

b

Words: 191 Articles: 1
4 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 191
b OurBigBook.com
Treat the two squares as a single edge-pairing construction, including the identifications between different squares. Number the corners of the left square counterclockwise from its lower left corner by A,B,C,D, and similarly use E,F,G,H on the right. The single arrows identify D with H and C with E. The double arrows identify G with F and H with G. The triple arrows identify A with E and B with F. The quadruple arrows identify A with C and D with B.
Thus there are precisely two vertex classes, {A,C,E} and {B,D,F,G,H}. There are four edge classes and two two-dimensional cells, so the resulting closed connected surface has Euler characteristic
χ=2−4+2=0.
(15)
It is a nonorientable surface: on the left square the quadruple-arrow sides have the same orientation relative to a traversal of its boundary, giving a twisted band after gluing. Equivalently, no choice of orientations for the two faces makes the induced directions opposite on every paired edge. The vertex links are circles, so these edge identifications produce a closed surface, rather than a singular cell space. The classification of compact surfaces now gives
Klein bottle.​
(16)
A torus also has Euler characteristic zero, but is excluded by the failed orientation test.

Differentiability at a means that there is a linear map L:V→V1​ with
∥h∥∥f(a+h)−f(a)−Lh∥1​​⟶0(h→0).
(17)
This map is the total derivative Dfa​. In the Frobenius norm, ∣AB∣≤∣A∣∣B∣, by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality applied to matrix entries. Expanding with the order of all factors preserved gives
(A+H)3=A3+A2H+AHA+HA2+AH2+HAH+H2A+H3.
(18)
The remainder after the terms linear in H has norm at most 3∣A∣∣H∣2+∣H∣3=o(∣H∣). Hence
DfA​(H)=A2H+AHA+HA2.​
(19)
For ∣C∣<1, the Neumann series I−C+C2−⋯ converges absolutely in the finite-dimensional space of matrices. Multiplying its partial sums by I+C and passing to the limit shows that it is (I+C)−1. Its remainder after I−C has norm at most ∣C∣2/(1−∣C∣)=o(∣C∣), proving the required expansion.
If A is an invertible matrix and ∣H∣<1/∣A−1∣, then A+H=A(I+A−1H) is an invertible matrix. Thus the general linear group is an open subset of the matrix space. The preceding expansion also gives
(A+H)−1=A−1−A−1HA−1+o(∣H∣).
(20)
Apply the chain rule to g(X)=(X−1)3, using the cubic total derivative at A−1 and this total derivative of inversion:
DgA​(H)=−A−3HA−1−A−2HA−2−A−1HA−3.​
(21)
The three terms generally cannot be combined by commuting A and H.

Parametrize the surface of revolution by
r(x,θ)=(x,y(x)cosθ,y(x)sinθ),0≤θ≤2π.
(22)
The magnitude of the cross product rx​×rθ​ is y1+y′2​. Integrating the surface area element over θ gives
J[y]=2π∫x1​x2​​y(x)1+y′(x)2​dx.​
(23)
Positivity of y removes an otherwise necessary absolute value in the area element.

ii

Words: 79 Articles: 1
2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 79
ii OurBigBook.com
For F(y,y′)=y1+y′2​, the Euler-Lagrange equation is
1+y′2​−dxd​1+y′2​yy′​=0,yy′′=1+y′2.
(24)
Since F has no explicit x dependence, the Beltrami identity gives
F−y′Fy′​=1+y′2​y​=C>0.
(25)
Solving this first integral, or substituting into the second-order equation, yields
y(x)=Ccosh(Cx−K​),C>0.​
(26)
The constants satisfy y1​=Ccosh((x1​−K)/C) and y2​=Ccosh((x2​−K)/C). There need not be a solution for arbitrary endpoint data, and when there is one these equations can have more than one pair of constants. These are the possible stationary catenoids, so the axisymmetric second variation of a catenoid still matters when deciding whether they minimize surface area.

iii

Words: 165 Articles: 1
2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 165
iii OurBigBook.com
The functional is unbounded above. Let ℓ be the positive affine interpolant of the endpoint values and choose a nonnegative, nonzero, continuously differentiable h vanishing at both endpoints. The admissible functions yM​=ℓ+Mh satisfy
J[yM​]≥2π∫x1​x2​​yM​dx⟶∞.
(27)
This excludes a global maximum, but does not prove that a stationary curve is a minimum. The concluding assertion is false without additional conditions.
An explicit counterexample uses x1​=−2, x2​=2, y1​=y2​=cosh2 and the stationary function y=coshx. Its second variation, for a perturbation h vanishing at the endpoints, is
2πδ2J[h]​=∫−22​(2tanhxhh′+sech2xh′2)dx=∫−22​sech2x(h′2−h2)dx.
(28)
Choose h=1−x2/4. Since sech2x≤4e−2∣x∣, the positive contribution is at most ∫R​x2e−2∣x∣dx=1/2. On [−1,1], h2≥9/16, so the magnitude of the negative contribution is at least (9/8)tanh1>9/16>1/2. Thus δ2J[h]<0. Small perturbations in this direction preserve positivity and the endpoint data while decreasing surface area. Consequently this catenoid is not a local minimum. The valid conclusion from part (ii) is a necessary stationary form; minimization requires a separate stability and existence analysis.

Write q=(x,X)T, M=(ab​bc​) and K=(αβ​βγ​). The Euler-Lagrange equations give Mq¨​+Kq=0. A normal mode is a motion q=vcos(ωt+φ) with fixed nonzero vector v; its normal frequency is ω>0. Substitution gives (K−ω2M)v=0. Thus the squared normal frequencies are the assumed positive distinct roots of
(ac−b2)λ2−(αc+γa−2βb)λ+(αγ−β2)=0.
(29)
For either root, solve the associated two linear equations for the mode ratio.
For the rods, the small angles are θ=x/a and ϕ=(X−x)/(2a). The first rod has kinetic energy mx˙2/6. The second rod's center has horizontal velocity (x˙+X˙)/2 and its angular velocity is (X˙−x˙)/(2a). Its center-of-mass moment of inertia is 2ma2/3, giving
T2​=4m​(x˙+X˙)2+12m​(X˙−x˙)2.
(30)
Adding these kinetic energies gives T=m(3x˙2+2x˙X˙+2X˙2)/6. The first center rises by aθ2/4, and the second by aθ2/2+aϕ2/2. Multiplying by the respective masses and g gives
V=4amg​[5x2+(X−x)2]=4amg​(6x2−2xX+X2).
(31)
Therefore the stated Lagrangian is T−V.
Set μ=2aω2/(3g). The mode equation is
det[(6−1​−11​)−μ(31​12​)]=5μ2−17μ+5=0.
(32)
Hence
ω±2​=20a3g​(17±321​).​
(33)
The mode ratio is r=X/x=(6−3μ)/(1+μ), so the ratio of the rods' angles is ϕ/θ=(r−1)/2=(5−4μ)/[2(1+μ)]. It is positive for μ−​=(17−321​)/10 and negative for μ+​=(17+321​)/10. Thus the lower-frequency normal mode has the rods in phase, and the higher-frequency normal mode has them out of phase.

2 OurBigBook.com
In vacuum, the source-free Maxwell equations are
∇⋅E=∇⋅B=0,∇×E=−∂t​B,∇×B=c−2∂t​E.
(34)
Put ψ=ω(t−z/c) and denote the constant electric amplitude by E0​. A corresponding traveling-wave magnetic field is
B=cE0​​(−sinψ,cosψ,0).​
(35)
Both divergences vanish because both the electric field and the magnetic field depend only on z,t and have zero z component. Direct differentiation gives ∇×E=(ωE0​/c)(cosψ,sinψ,0)=−∂t​B and ∇×B=(ωE0​/c2)(−sinψ,cosψ,0)=c−2∂t​E. A time-independent background magnetic field satisfying the homogeneous equations could be added; the formula is the wave component.
Introduce the magnetic vector potential and electric potential by B=∇×A and E=−∇ϕ−∂t​A. These identities automatically give the divergence equation for B and Faraday's law. For this wave choose ϕ=0 and A=(c/ω)B; the derivatives just calculated verify both potential equations.
The electromagnetic force is the Lorentz force, Q(E+v×B). On the smooth constraint plane z=z0​, the constraint force is normal to the plane. Both v and B are tangential, so v×B is normal and is balanced by that constraint force; it does not affect the tangential motion. Thus
r¨∥​=mQE0​​(cosψ,sinψ).
(36)
A particular motion is r∥​=r0​−[QE0​/(mω2)](cosψ,sinψ), a circle of radius
mω2∣QE0​∣​.​
(37)
The general planar motion also includes a constant drift velocity; the particle moves on a circle when that drift is zero. The constraint force can do no work because it is perpendicular to the velocity.

σn​∑k=1n​Uk​−nμ​ d​ N(0,1).

For W=−log(1−Y), P(W≤w)=1−e−w when w≥0, and it is zero otherwise. Therefore its probability density function is e−wχ(0,∞)​(w): the exponential distribution of rate one. By integration by parts, E[W]=1 and E[W2]=2, so Var(W)=1.
The variables Wk​=−log(1−Fk​(Xk​)) are independent because they are separate measurable functions of independent random variables. The probability integral transform makes all of them identically distributed as Exp(1), even though the Xk​ need not be identically distributed. The displayed Zn​ is exactly n−1/2∑k=1n​(Wk​−1). The second part of the Gershgorin circle theorem states that if a union of k of the discs is disjoint from every remaining disc, that union contains exactly k eigenvalues, counted with algebraic multiplicity. For 0<ϵ<1/4 and δ<(n−1)/2−ϵ, the Gershgorin discs from rows have one enlarged component on the left; the Gershgorin discs from columns have one enlarged component on the right. Thus, when n=2m, every disc with index at most m is isolated in the column family and every disc with index at least m+1 is isolated in the row family. Their counts give all n eigenvalues, one in each disjoint small disc, so all are real.
When n=2m+1, the same argument isolates the first m discs in the column family and the last m in the row family. It accounts for 2m real eigenvalues. The one remaining eigenvalue is real by conjugation, and belongs to the central small disc: the enlarged left and right discs are disjoint, and their two components can intersect only within the disc centered at m+1. The Petersen graph has ten vertices, fifteen edges, and girth five. One way to verify the girth is its description by the two-element subsets of a five-element set, with adjacency meaning disjointness. A triangle would require three pairwise disjoint two-element subsets, which is impossible. Two distinct vertices have at most one common neighbor: the only possible common neighbor is a two-element subset of the complement of their union. Therefore a four-cycle is impossible. A five-cycle exists in its standard pentagon drawing.
If it were a planar graph, part (i) would give 15≤(5/3)(10−2)=40/3, a contradiction. Thus the Petersen graph is nonplanar. The held source has blank space where its drawing is mentioned; the named graph determines this argument without that missing illustration.

Increase u2​,u3​ by two and decrease v2​ by two. The new tight edge (3,4) reaches an unmatched column. Augment along 2→2→3→4, replacing (3,2) by (2,2),(3,4). The matching becomes {(1,1),(2,2),(3,4),(5,3)}.
Now grow from unmatched row four. Edge (4,1) reaches matched row one, and edge (1,5) reaches unmatched column five. Augment along 4→1→1→5, replacing (1,1) by (4,1),(1,5). This yields
{(1,5),(2,2),(3,4),(4,1),(5,3)},cost 2.​

Before a potential update, let S be the reached rows and T the reached columns in an alternating forest grown from unmatched rows. Every reached column is matched, or an augmentation would already have occurred, and its matched row is reached. Each tree has one more reached row than reached column, so ∣S∣−∣T∣>0.
The update amount is the smallest slack across S×Tc. It is strictly positive because all zero-slack edges have already been explored, and the complete assignment problem guarantees that the set is nonempty before a perfect matching is found. Increasing ui​ for i∈S and decreasing vj​ for j∈T therefore increases the dual sum by
Δ(∣S∣−∣T∣)>0.​
(82)
All feasibility inequalities remain valid by the definition of the minimum slack.
